summary:
ASTRA EXPLORER is an interactive planetary exploration platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, addressing the challenge “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.”

The project aims to identify Earth locations that share geological, topographical, and environmental characteristics with selected regions on the Moon and Mars. It combines planetary datasets, terrain analysis, and climate information to explore similarities and differences between extraterrestrial environments and potential terrestrial analogs.

ASTRA EXPLORER features interactive 3D exploration of Earth, the Moon, and Mars, allowing users to investigate selected planetary regions and their corresponding Earth analog locations. It integrates scientific data from NASA sources, including LOLA lunar elevation data, MOLA Martian elevation data, and NASA POWER climate datasets.

Built using Python, FastAPI, Next.js, TypeScript, and CesiumJS, the platform processes scientific data and presents it through an accessible interactive interface. Planned terrain comparisons include elevation, slope, surface roughness, and data uncertainty.

By connecting planetary science with real-world locations on Earth, ASTRA EXPLORER helps users understand the challenges of future lunar and Martian exploration. Its comparisons are exploratory and highlight environmental similarities and differences rather than claiming perfect equivalents.
details:
ASTRA EXPLORER — Bridging Worlds Through Planetary Analog Research

Project Overview

ASTRA EXPLORER is an interactive planetary exploration and comparative research platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It addresses a fundamental challenge in future space exploration: identifying and evaluating terrestrial environments that exhibit meaningful geological, topographical, and environmental similarities to selected regions on the Moon and Mars.

As humanity prepares for sustained lunar exploration and future crewed missions to Mars, understanding extraterrestrial surface conditions becomes increasingly important. Earth provides accessible natural environments that can serve as scientific analogs for studying terrain, environmental extremes, geological processes, and operational challenges. However, identifying meaningful analogs requires more than visual resemblance. It requires measurable data, spatial analysis, and an understanding of the limitations of cross-planetary comparisons.

ASTRA EXPLORER aims to bring these elements together in one interactive, data-driven environment.

How It Works

The platform connects three planetary environments through an integrated geospatial exploration interface: Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Users can explore planetary surfaces, select reference regions, and investigate their corresponding terrestrial analog locations. The system combines scientific datasets, geospatial processing, and interactive visualization to transform complex planetary information into an accessible research experience.

Its scientific workflow is based on three complementary data domains:

1. Lunar Terrain Analysis

ASTRA EXPLORER integrates Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) datasets from NASA's Planetary Geosciences Data Archive. These include high-resolution south-polar elevation models, slope products, and uncertainty information.

The platform uses these products to investigate lunar surface elevation and terrain characteristics around scientifically relevant regions, including Haworth, de Gerlache Rim, and Malapert Massif. The inclusion of uncertainty data is particularly important because it helps distinguish measured information from limitations in the underlying terrain models.

2. Martian Topographical Exploration

For Mars, the platform processes Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) Mission Experiment Gridded Data Record (MEGDR) elevation data. Its global elevation raster allows the system to retrieve topographical measurements at selected Martian coordinates.

Reference regions include Gale Crater, Jezero Crater, and Olympus Mons, providing different geographical and geological contexts for planetary exploration.

3. Terrestrial Environmental Analysis

For Earth, ASTRA EXPLORER integrates NASA POWER meteorological datasets through its API, currently using daily near-surface air temperature (T2M).

Selected terrestrial locations can be investigated through their geographic coordinates and historical temperature records. This creates a foundation for comparing environmental characteristics between Earth analog candidates and extraterrestrial reference environments, while recognizing that terrestrial atmospheric measurements cannot directly represent lunar or Martian surface conditions.

Scientific Methodology and Comparative Analysis

A central principle of ASTRA EXPLORER is that planetary analog identification should be based on measurable characteristics rather than visual similarity alone.

The platform's comparative research direction includes:

  • Elevation distribution and regional topography.
  • Surface slope and terrain variability.
  • Terrain roughness and local relief.
  • Temperature patterns and environmental extremes.
  • Spatial coverage, dataset resolution, and measurement uncertainty.

These parameters must be evaluated using compatible spatial scales and appropriate scientific assumptions. For example, absolute elevations across Earth, the Moon, and Mars cannot be compared directly without considering their different reference datums and vertical coordinate systems.

Likewise, comparing a high-resolution lunar DEM with a much coarser Martian elevation product requires resolution-aware processing. The platform therefore treats dataset quality, spatial coverage, coordinate transformations, and uncertainty as essential parts of the research process.

The long-term objective is to develop a transparent, data-driven analog comparison framework that evaluates multiple characteristics instead of relying on a single measurement or arbitrary similarity score.

Technology and Engineering Architecture

ASTRA EXPLORER is developed using a modern full-stack architecture combining web engineering, scientific computing, and geospatial visualization.

Frontend and Visualization

  • Next.js and React for the application architecture and user interface.
  • TypeScript for structured, maintainable application logic.
  • CesiumJS for interactive three-dimensional planetary and geospatial exploration.
  • NASA planetary imagery and tile services for visual surface representation.

Backend and Scientific Computing

  • Python for scientific data processing.
  • FastAPI for RESTful API development and communication between the frontend and scientific services.
  • Rasterio for reading and processing geospatial raster datasets.
  • NumPy and SciPy for numerical analysis and scientific computation.
  • PyProj for coordinate transformations and geospatial reference-system operations.
  • HTTPX for asynchronous communication with external scientific APIs.

Scientific Data Infrastructure

  • NASA LOLA elevation, slope, and uncertainty products.
  • NASA MOLA global Martian elevation data.
  • NASA POWER daily meteorological data.
  • NASA Trek planetary imagery services.

The architecture separates the interactive application from scientific data processing, allowing the platform to expand as additional datasets and analytical capabilities are integrated.

Innovation and Creativity

The primary innovation of ASTRA EXPLORER is its effort to connect planetary exploration with terrestrial analog research through a unified, interactive geospatial experience.

Instead of treating Earth, the Moon, and Mars as isolated visualization subjects, the project approaches them as interconnected environments that can be investigated through common scientific questions.

Its distinguishing characteristics include:

  • Cross-planetary exploration: Bringing three planetary environments into one interactive platform.
  • Data-driven investigation: Using real NASA scientific datasets rather than relying exclusively on illustrative representations.
  • Multi-parameter comparison: Exploring terrain and environmental characteristics together.
  • Scientific transparency: Considering uncertainty, spatial coverage, resolution, and coordinate-system differences.
  • Accessibility: Making planetary data easier to explore and understand through an interactive visual interface.

This approach creates an opportunity to connect planetary science, Earth science, geospatial engineering, and computer science within one educational and research-oriented platform.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA EXPLORER aims to contribute to several areas:

Planetary Science and Research: It provides an accessible environment for exploring planetary datasets and investigating potential terrestrial analogs for lunar and Martian regions.

Future Space Exploration: By helping users understand similarities and differences between terrestrial and extraterrestrial terrain, the platform can support preliminary research into environments relevant to future exploration planning. It is not intended to certify landing-site safety or establish operational suitability.

STEM Education: The platform transforms complex scientific concepts such as laser altimetry, digital elevation models, geospatial coordinate systems, raster analysis, and environmental data into an interactive learning experience.

Open Scientific Data Utilization: It demonstrates how publicly available NASA datasets and APIs can be integrated into practical software applications, encouraging broader engagement with open scientific resources.

Future Development: The architecture provides a foundation for incorporating additional geological datasets, higher-resolution terrain products, more environmental parameters, advanced spatial statistics, and scientifically validated analog-ranking methodologies.

Factors Considered During Development

Scientific reliability and responsible interpretation have guided the project's development.

The team considered:

  • Authenticity and traceability of scientific datasets.
  • Geographic coverage of selected planetary regions.
  • Differences between planetary coordinate systems and reference datums.
  • Variations in spatial resolution between datasets.
  • Elevation and slope measurement uncertainty.
  • The distinction between visual similarity and scientifically meaningful analogy.
  • API reliability, data-processing performance, and application scalability.
  • Accessibility and clarity of scientific information for users with different levels of technical knowledge.

These considerations help ensure that the platform presents scientific information responsibly rather than overstating the conclusions that can be drawn from available data.

Vision

ASTRA EXPLORER aims to become more than a planetary visualization application. Its long-term vision is to evolve into an extensible planetary analog research environment where users can explore extraterrestrial landscapes, investigate terrestrial environments, compare scientific measurements, and understand the challenges of exploring worlds beyond Earth.

By combining NASA's open scientific resources with modern software engineering and geospatial analysis, ASTRA EXPLORER seeks to make the relationship between our planet and other worlds more understandable, measurable, and accessible.

Explore Earth. Investigate the Moon. Discover Mars. Connect worlds through science.
